Q: SQL joins fail to produce nice way to access data from query A:

I'll explain with an analogy. Forget SQL for a moment.

Consider two sets: cities and baseball teams. Each entry is one city or one team name.

{
 Chicago
 Los Angeles
 New York
}

{
 Angels
 Cubs
 Mets
 White Sox
 Yankees
}

A reasonable join between these two sets would be cities coupled with their respective home team. Each entry of this result has one element from each set. Always one city with one team.

{
 Chicago / Cubs
 Chicago / White Sox
 Los Angeles / Angels
 New York / Mets
 New York / Yankees
}

This is what JOIN does. Even though it city name appear multiple times, it's a useful result because it can be used in further comparisons, conditions, or other operations.

For example, if you want a condition like WHERE team != 'Yankees' the first example would eliminate New York / Yankees but it would still include New York / Mets.

It seems you want the sets to be nested, so each city would appear only once, and the matching teams would be combined into a kind of nested set:

{
 Chicago / { Cubs, White Sox }
 Los Angeles / { Angels }
 New York / { Mets, Yankees }
}

But this would be harder to use in further relational operations. If you apply the condition on team != 'Yankees', should it eliminate only part of the element for New York, or the whole element? Either could be right for one application, and the opposite could be right for another application.

Likewise if you want to join the result to a third set. How to combine nested sets? It becomes very unclear.

Joins produce "flat" sets of rows, consisting of all the columns from two tables. They do this to make it simpler to use the result in further relational operations.

I understand this is not convenient for your current programming task, because the columns from t1 appear redundant, and you have to process them somehow.

This does not mean join is misbehaving. It's working the way it was intended.

I wrote more about using joins effectively in a chapter of my book, More SQL Antipatterns.

Q: Beyond Next Token Prediction: Integrating System 2 Thinking for AGI-level Reasonin? A:

Fascinating topic, Peter. As an AI Architect, I've seen that while scaling NTP (Next Token Prediction) yields emergent behaviors, it doesn't solve the "Causal Gap." 🌍🤖

System 2 thinking—specifically through "Spec-Driven Development" (SDD) and verifiable reasoning traces—is the essential hedge. In the German Mittelstand, we can't rely on stochastic parrots for sensitive industrial logic. We need "Sovereign Reasoning" where the model's multi-step planning is constrained by a human-parseable technical spec before execution.

Scaling might give us more "System 1" intuition, but AGI requires the auditable verification that only symbolic or structured reasoning (System 2) can provide. 🚀 #SovereignAI #AGI #SDD #System2Thinking

Q: Excel Cell Date Format is not correct A:

It appears as though your date column has a combination of properly formatted dates, and text strings that look like dates.

Assumptions:

Due to the cropping of your screenshot, it is unclear which column in your data set contains the dates. I will use column "D" in my solution below.

Due to the limited sample size of the incorrectly formatted dates, it is unclear if they should be interpreted as MM/DD/YYYY or DD/MM/YYYY. I will assume they are DD/MM/YYYY in my solution below.

Solution:

Insert a new column to the right of your Date column. To do this, right-click on the column header "E" and select "Insert".

Next, format the new column "E" as a "Short Date". To do this, on the Ribbon go to the Home Tab > Number Group and select "Short Date" from the Number Format drop down list.

In cell E2, use the following formula, then copy it down to the bottom of the data set:

=IF(ISNUMBER(D2), D2, DATE(RIGHT(TRIM(D2),4), MID(D2,FIND("/",D2)+1,2), LEFT(TRIM(D2),2)))

Verify the new dates are correct. You can then Copy and Paste Special > Values, to overwrite the formulas with the correct date values.

UPDATED:

If I'm not mistaken "nous avons rencontré une erreur dans cette formule" is French, non?

If so, the Excel function equivalents applicable to this solution are as follows:

English French
IF SI
ISNUMBER ESTNUM
DATE DATE
LEFT GAUCHE
RIGHT DROITE
MID STXT
FIND TROUVE
TRIM SUPPRESPACE

Source: https://www.perfectxl.com

If I've translated it correctly, the French version for the solution above should be:

=SI(ESTNUM(D2), D2, DATE(DROITE(SUPPRESPACE(D2),4), STXT(D2,TROUVE("/",D2)+1,2), GAUCHE(SUPPRESPACE(D2),2)))

I hope that works! ;-)

Q: Can't figure out the real way to learn the C++ language? A:

C++ is a lot. It's definitely not the language to start with learning on (late 1990s AP CS course design to the contrary); even with all the improvements in the latest language/library standards (of which std::span is one), it's something I'd ease into. Reading the standard is unusually taxing, because it is basically written in an alien language (one designed to be precise at the expense of friendliness), even to native English speakers, and it's extra difficult if English is your second language, and especially if you're trying to eat the elephant all in one byte (e.g. digging into each and every template parameter on common types, even when they're defaulted).

So my first suggestion is, when reading cppreference.com, to not focus on learning every corner of a new type (especially not defaulted parameters) all at once. Read example code for the type, get a basic idea of the what and why, before focusing on the nitty-gritty how. If you don't know why a tool exists, and what it's for, trying to learn how it works is jumping the gun. In the case of std::span, the short "what" is "it's a view of data stored 'somewhere else'". The "why" is "because 99% of the time, data being passed around doesn't need to be in a formal container type, with known rules for growing and shrinking, adding and removing, etc., and it's more efficient, both for the program and the developer, to write APIs that do nothing but pass along a view of (a portion of) the data when all that is needed is that view". Before std::span, your main options for passing around simple contiguous data that won't be resized were:

  1. Write a templated function receiving a possibly-const reference to the data; the templating makes it only a little uglier, but it also means the function gets recompiled into multiple versions depending on how it's used, e.g. it might end up specialized for C-style arrays, std::array of each possibly compile-time size, std::vector, etc. (and now your code is bloated by each copy, even though the discrete copies generally won't buy meaningful performance benefits, and it means a single logically "hot" function might be split into a dozen "cold" implementations, harming cache efficacy). And if the caller wanted to only pass some elements of the data in, they'd need to copy them (and copy them back if the callee was supposed to mutate them) to a single data structure.
  2. Receive a pointer to type + length (or equivalently, pointer to first and last element, or iterator to first and last element, though the iterator case means we're back to templates) to support the "pass only some elements" case cheaply, but now the language can't easily check your accesses (the pointer and length aren't directly related), the ownership semantics are not clear from the API (a raw pointer doesn't properly express anything about ownership), and it's much easier to make mistakes (oops, I offset the start pointer but didn't reduce the total length to match).
  3. Manually implementing it for each specific supported type (avoiding template headaches by adding reimplementation headaches), but still not working with subranges of the input without copies.

std::span solves this by letting you write a single, non-templated (or less templated) function that just receives a std::span by value, without regard to the specific container storing the data (the same code path can be used for any contiguous data structure the caller might have, and for any subset of that data they care to limit it to). Now your function is simpler (no receiving information about the subview side-band in length or end arguments), more efficient (no copy-of-template-per-container type), and more flexible (e.g. if you want the callee to work on all but the first element of a collection, for most collections, if it's known to be non-empty, you just do std::span(mycollection).subspan(1) and pass that, with std::span and .subspan doing the necessary pointer manipulation.

The main quirk with it is that it's designed to allow maximum optimization, thus supporting both static (fixed at compile time) and dynamic (determined at runtime) extents. If you initially use it with nothing but dynamic extents (the default), you're fine, just possibly suboptimal, but you can look into it deeper later on if you end up with a project where profiling shows span-related code to be a bottleneck.

If you've been taught C++ formally (no glaring gaps in the fundamentals, but perhaps taught against early language standards, or focused on C-like usage rather than idiomatic use of the standard library), you'll get there eventually. But it'll be easier if you try to learn several languages first, especially ones which force specific idioms on you (e.g. regex in Perl, functional programming in Lisp or Haskell, raw pointer use in plain C, OOP in Java, event loops in JS, iterators in Python, ownership semantics in Rust, etc.), and you learn to use them idiomatically. The reason I suggest this is two-fold:

  1. C++ is a multiparadigm language. If your only exposure to programming is through a single multiparadigm language, you'll generally end up with glaring gaps in your skills, because you won't even know the gaps exist (if you learn C++ without focusing on pointers, which is mostly possible in the modern standards, your mental model for half the language will be broken). Forcing yourself to learn idiomatic programming in other languages makes you better in all languages, simply because you have more programming "tools" in your mental toolkit, making it easier to solve problems in the way most appropriate to the problem at hand, rather than, to stretch the metaphor, trying to hammer in nails with the butt end of a screwdriver.
  2. Once you've learned enough languages, quickly enough, your brain reshapes itself; instead of learning a language as a single monolithic thing, isolated from every other language you've learned, you start to think on two levels, the syntax and idioms of each language, mapped onto an underlying substrate of programming concepts. Each new language adds only a tiny handful of things to the latter, and you just learn new mappings of the former for the new language.

For something like std::span, it immediately made sense to me because:

  1. It builds on the initial steps taken with std::string_view (a read-only, string-focused precursor to std::span); I paid attention to the big features in each new C++ standard, so familiarity with std::string_view meant less of a leap to std::span.
  2. I've worked in Rust, which provides a slice type that is basically std::span integrated into the language on a syntactic level; it's near impossible to learn Rust without internalizing knowledge of how slices work, and that knowledge translates pretty directly to C++'s std::span (even if it's rather less pretty, syntactically, in C++).

If all I knew was pre-C++11 C++, which is all I've been formally taught (you can forgive my professors; when I was in school, the latest C++ standard was C++03), and had little or no experience with other languages, yeah, trying to figure out std::span would be a nightmare. I get how it can be intimidating try to read formal spec-ese (or even the lightly friendlier spec-ese cppreference.com uses) for a language feature you don't understand. Don't do it. Take classes to learn the core material. Look up tutorials to learn new individual libraries and features. Then dive into the spec-ese weeds if you're so inclined.
